slides.lead: Fed, changed, rocked, and still crying at 6 weeks?
slides.sub: Is this much crying normal? Here is the real range.

slides.head: About 2 hours of fussing and crying a day is average in the first 6 weeks

range.mostLabel: Weeks 0 to 6: about 2 hours of fussing and crying a day
range.markLabel: Weeks 10 to 12: about 68 minutes a day

slides.body: From parent diaries of 8,690 babies in 28 studies (Wolke, 2017). Across studies there was no single sharp peak at 6 weeks, more a hard early stretch that eases.

slides.head: Colic is common early, then rare

stat.label: of babies cry enough to count as colic in the first 6 weeks

slides.body:
By 10 to 12 weeks, it is 0.6%.

The catch: these are parents' diary records. One small study that used recorders on 20 babies measured far less crying.

slides.head: It is not a sign you are doing it wrong
slides.body:
Persistent crying at 6 weeks usually happens even with a sensitive, affectionate mother (St James-Roberts, 1998).

And most heavy criers at 5 to 6 weeks were settled at night by 12 weeks (St James-Roberts, 2011).

slides.head: Your baby has very few ways to calm down alone
slides.body:
Self-control grows out of being calmed by someone else. The brain's own brakes take charge at about 3 to 4 years (Rothbart, 2011).

For now, a baby's main tool of their own is looking away. Much of the rest, they borrow from you.

slides.head: Worth asking your pediatrician about
items: Crying with a fever, poor feeding or vomiting, or a cry unlike their usual one. Call, rather than wait.
Crying that is not easing by about 3 months
Anything that feels wrong to you, at any age
slides.note: Not a diagnosis. Asking calmly is never overreacting.

slides.head: On the hard evenings
items: Catch fussing early: dim the lights, let them look away.
Hold them and walk around instead of sitting.
Trade off, so the calmer adult holds them.
At your edge, lay them on their back in the crib, step out, breathe, go back when you are steady.
